privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: How ResuMax collects, uses, and protects your personal data — written in plain language, with the same rights extended to every user worldwide.

keyPoints.title: We never sell your data
keyPoints.description: We do not sell or share your personal information for advertising, and we never have.

keyPoints.title: Your resume stays yours

keyPoints.title: Delete everything, anytime

keyPoints.title: Full rights, everywhere

blocks.text: ResuMax is a resume and CV building platform operated by FALO Enterprise (“we”, “us”, “our”). This Privacy Policy explains what personal data we collect when you use resumax.io, why we collect it, who we share it with, and the control you have over it.

We have written this in plain language deliberately. Where a legal term is unavoidable we define it inline. If anything here is unclear, email us at <mail>privacy@resumax.io</mail> and we will explain it.

blocks.title: One standard for everyone
blocks.text: Rather than giving different rights to users in different countries, we extend the protections of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to every user of ResuMax, worldwide. Regional laws that grant you additional rights still apply on top — see Regional rights.
We collect only what the product needs to function. There are four categories:

items.text: Your name, email address, and profile picture. If you set a password, we store it hashed with Argon2 — a one-way function, meaning we cannot read your password and cannot recover it for you. We also store your email verification status and your notification preferences.

Everything you enter into the builder: contact details, work experience, education, certifications, skills, projects, and your professional summary. This is the most sensitive data we hold, and we treat it accordingly.

Your subscription plan, status, and renewal dates, plus identifiers issued by our payment processor. We never see or store your card number — see Who we share data with. We also count your AI generations and document downloads to enforce plan limits.

Standard server logs (IP address, browser type, timestamps) needed to operate the service securely, and short-lived security tokens for password resets and sign-in links. Those tokens are stored hashed, never in plain text.

blocks.title: What we deliberately do not collect
blocks.text: We do not collect biometric data, precise location, government identifiers, or any special-category data such as health, religion, or political affiliation. If you choose to type such information into a resume field, it is processed only as ordinary resume content — please avoid entering more than a prospective employer needs.

sections.title: 3. How we use your data and why we are allowed to

blocks.text: Under the GDPR every use of personal data needs a lawful basis. This table sets out ours in full.

rows: Contract — necessary to provide the service you signed up for
Build, store, and export your resumes
Generate resume text with AI when you ask
Send service emails (verification, password resets, plan changes)
Send product news, if you opt in
Consent — withdrawable at any time in Settings
Keep the service secure and prevent abuse
Fix bugs and improve the product

blocks.title: We do not profile or advertise
blocks.text: We do not use your data for automated decision-making that produces legal effects, we do not build advertising profiles, and we do not run third-party ad trackers on resumax.io.

When you use an AI-assisted feature — generating a summary, rewriting a bullet point, tailoring a resume to a role — the relevant portion of your resume content is sent to Google Gemini, operated by Google LLC, which returns the generated text. We want you to know this explicitly rather than bury it.

items: Only what is needed is sent. We transmit the fields relevant to your request, not your entire account.
Your content is not used to train models. We use Google's paid enterprise API, under terms that prohibit using submitted data to train or improve their models.
AI features are opt-in per action. Nothing is sent to an AI provider unless you press a button that asks for it.
Output is a draft, not advice. AI-generated text can be inaccurate. You are responsible for verifying that everything on your resume is truthful — see our Terms.

blocks.text: We do not sell your personal data, and we never have. We share it only with the service providers below, each of which processes data on our instructions under a written agreement. This is our complete list of subprocessors.

rows: Payment processing and subscription billing, acting as Merchant of Record
Name, email, billing country, transaction records. Card details go directly to Paddle and never reach our servers.
AI text generation, when you request it
The resume fields relevant to your request
“Sign in with Google”, if you choose it
Your Google account identifier, name, email, and profile picture
Running the application and storing your data

blocks.text: Your resume PDFs are rendered on our own infrastructure. They are not sent to any third-party document service.

We may also disclose data where legally compelled — a valid court order or binding request from a competent authority — or to establish or defend legal claims. If we are permitted to notify you of such a request, we will. If FALO Enterprise is involved in a merger or acquisition, your data may transfer to the successor entity under this same policy, and we will notify you before it takes effect.
ResuMax does not run advertising or third-party analytics cookies. We use only what the product needs to work:

rows: Keeps you signed in between visits
Remembers whether you chose light or dark mode
Remembers your language and reduced-motion setting
Prevents losing work in progress if your connection drops

blocks.text: Because none of these are used for tracking or advertising, no consent banner is required. Clearing your browser storage removes the functional items; you will simply be signed out and your preferences reset to default.

rows: Until you delete your account, plus up to 30 days in backups
Up to 7 years after the transaction, as tax law requires
Expire within hours; deleted after use

blocks.text: When you delete your account, your resumes, drafts, and linked sign-in accounts are erased immediately from our live systems by cascade deletion. Encrypted backups roll off within 30 days. We retain only the billing records tax law obliges us to keep.
These rights apply to every ResuMax user, wherever you live:

items.text: Get a copy of the personal data we hold about you.
Correct anything inaccurate. Most fields you can edit yourself in the dashboard.
Delete your account and all associated data. Available immediately in Settings → Privacy — you do not need to ask us.
Receive your resume data in a structured, machine-readable format, or export any resume as a document.
Ask us to pause processing, or object to processing we base on legitimate interests.
Turn off marketing email at any time in Settings. Withdrawing consent does not affect processing already carried out.
Lodge a complaint with your local data protection authority. We would appreciate the chance to resolve it first.

blocks.text: To exercise any right, email privacy@resumax.io. We respond within 30 days, free of charge. We will never charge you a fee or degrade your service for exercising a right.
If you live in California, the CCPA as amended by the CPRA gives you specific rights. They are already covered by the section above, but named here in the statute's own terms:

items: Right to know what personal information we collect, use, and disclose.
Right to delete the personal information we hold about you.
Right to correct inaccurate personal information.
Right to opt out of sale or sharing. We do not sell or share personal information, so there is nothing to opt out of — including for users under 16.
Right to limit use of sensitive personal information. We do not collect sensitive personal information as the CPRA defines it.
Right to non-discrimination — we will never charge you more or give you less for exercising these rights.

faqs.question: How do I build my first resume?
faqs.answer: Create an account, answer the short setup survey, and you will land in the dashboard with a draft already started. Fill in each section — contact, experience, education, skills — and your resume updates live in the preview beside it. You can change template at any point without losing anything you have written.

faqs.question: Is ResuMax free to use?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Free plan lets you build and preview a resume with no credit card. Paid plans add unlimited exports, watermark-free PDFs, and the premium template library. You can compare everything on the Pricing page.

faqs.question: Can I write my resume in Arabic?
faqs.answer: Yes. ResuMax is fully bilingual and supports right-to-left layout throughout, so Arabic resumes render correctly in every template. Switch language from the toggle in the top navigation at any time.

faqs.question: Does the AI write my resume for me?
faqs.answer: It writes drafts, not final copy. When you ask for help, the relevant part of your resume is sent to Google Gemini, which suggests wording you can accept, edit, or discard. Always review what it produces — AI can overstate experience or invent detail, and everything on your resume needs to be true.

faqs.question: Is my resume used to train AI models?
faqs.answer: No. We use Google's paid enterprise API under terms that prohibit using submitted content to train or improve their models. Your resume is never sold, published, or shared with recruiters. This is set out in full in our Privacy Policy.

faqs.question: Will my resume pass ATS screening?
faqs.answer: Our templates are built with clean, parseable structure and avoid the layout tricks that commonly break applicant tracking systems. That said, no tool can guarantee any specific system will accept a document — ATS behaviour varies by employer, so treat it as strong preparation rather than a promise.

faqs.question: Why isn't my resume downloading as a PDF?
faqs.answer: Most often it is a browser blocking the download, or an export limit reached on the Free plan. Check your browser's download permissions first, then confirm your plan allows PDF export. If both look fine, message us below with the resume title and we will look at it directly.

faqs.question: How do I remove the watermark from my resume?
faqs.answer: The watermark applies to exports on the Free plan. Upgrading to a paid plan removes it from every export immediately — you do not need to rebuild or re-export anything you have already written.

faqs.question: What payment methods do you accept?
faqs.answer: Payments are handled by Paddle, our Merchant of Record, which accepts major credit and debit cards along with regional payment methods depending on your country. Paddle also handles any VAT or sales tax due. We never see or store your card details.

faqs.question: How do I cancel my subscription?
faqs.answer: Open Settings, go to Billing, and cancel there. Your plan stays active until the end of the period you have already paid for, and you will not be charged again. Cancelling does not delete your resumes.

faqs.question: Can I switch plans later?
faqs.answer: Yes, at any time. Upgrades take effect immediately so you get the new features straight away. Downgrades take effect at the start of your next billing cycle, and your existing resumes stay in your account either way.

faqs.question: I didn't get my verification email.
faqs.answer: Check your spam or promotions folder first, since automated mail often lands there. You can request a new code from the verification screen. If nothing arrives after a few minutes, message us with the email address you signed up with and we will verify the account manually.

faqs.question: How do I delete my account and my data?
faqs.answer: Go to Settings, then Privacy, and use Delete account. This permanently erases your account, resumes, and drafts from our live systems straight away, and encrypted backups roll off within 30 days. You do not need to email us to request it.

faqs.question: Can I sign in with Google?
faqs.answer: Yes. Choose “Continue with Google” on the sign-in or sign-up screen. If you already registered with a password using the same email address, the two are linked to one account, so you can use either method.

faqs.question: I lost work when my connection dropped.
faqs.answer: Drafts are saved to your browser as you type, so reopening the builder on the same device usually restores what you had. If it does not come back, tell us roughly when you were working and what you were editing, and we will check whether a server-side draft can be recovered.

faqs.question: My exported PDF looks different from the preview.
faqs.answer: This is nearly always a font or page-break difference on very long content. Try shortening overflowing sections or switching template, and re-export. If it still does not match, send us the resume title and a screenshot of the difference so we can reproduce it.

about.title: A resume should say what you actually did.
about.subtitle: ResuMax is a resume builder for people applying across borders — built around the standards recruiters and screening software actually use, not the ones the internet guesses at.
about.metaDescription: ResuMax is a bilingual, standards-first resume builder by FALO Enterprise, built for people applying across borders.

story.title: It started with a document nobody could agree on

chapters.title: The same document, rejected for five different reasons

blocks.text: A resume is one of the few documents you are expected to write well, with no training, no feedback, and no way to know why it failed. Send the same file to five employers in three countries and you can be rejected five times for reasons that contradict each other — too long here, missing a photo there, badly parsed by software you never saw.

The advice available is worse than the problem. Most of it is confidently wrong, region-blind, and written for a job market that stopped existing a decade ago. Meanwhile the actual constraint — that your file has to survive being turned into database rows before a human ever reads it — barely gets mentioned.

chapters.title: So we started from the standards instead

blocks.text: We built ResuMax the other way round: begin with what each region's employers and screening systems actually expect, encode that into the templates and the guidance, and let the writing happen inside those rails. A Gulf employer and a German one want genuinely different documents. Pretending otherwise is the single most common way a strong candidate gets filtered out.
The goal was never to make a resume that sounds impressive. It was to make one that survives the process and still sounds like you.

That principle decided most of the hard calls. It is why the AI edits your sentence rather than replacing it, why it will ask you for a number instead of inventing one, and why ResuMax will not help you inflate a job title. A resume that wins an interview you cannot survive is not a feature.

ResuMax is built by a small team at FALO Enterprise, and it is early — version 1.0 is what ships today, and the roadmap below is the honest version of what comes next rather than a list of things already finished. The product is fully bilingual in English and Arabic, right-to-left included, because that was a requirement from the first commit and not a translation added later.

If something on the page is wrong, or a template does not match what employers in your country expect, tell us at <mail>hello@resumax.io</mail>. A person reads it, and regional corrections are the feedback we act on fastest.

honesty.title: Honesty first
honesty.description: ResuMax enforces truthful representation — no inflated job titles, no fabricated credentials. It means we decline a request users sometimes genuinely want, on the grounds that an interview you cannot back up is worse than no interview.

ats.title: ATS-first structure
ats.description: Every template is engineered to survive being parsed into database fields, because that happens before a person reads a word. It rules out a category of beautiful layouts that quietly destroy their own content on the way in.

relevance.title: Relevance over length
relevance.description: Guided word limits and section priorities keep documents concise and impact-driven. It means the tool will push back when you add a tenth bullet point to a role from nine years ago.

cultural.description: Region-specific guidance on photos, age, marital status and length. There is no universally correct resume, so we refuse to ship one default and call it global.

privacy.description: You control exactly what personal data appears and how it is stored. Resume drafts are not training data — our AI runs on an enterprise agreement that contractually forbids it.

ats-resume-checklist.title: The ATS checklist: nine things to fix before you apply
ats-resume-checklist.excerpt: Applicant tracking systems reject far fewer resumes than the internet claims — but the ones they do reject tend to fail for the same nine reasons.

blocks.text: An applicant tracking system is a database, not a judge. It stores applications, parses each file into structured fields — name, employer, dates, skills — and lets a recruiter search that pile. The parsing step is where resumes fail, and it fails quietly: nothing bounces, your experience simply lands in the wrong column or nowhere at all.

blocks.title: The myth worth dropping
blocks.text: No mainstream ATS assigns your resume a secret score and bins it below a threshold. A human still opens the shortlist. What the software decides is whether you appear in that shortlist when someone searches for your skill.
That reframes the whole problem. You are not trying to please an algorithm. You are trying to be findable, and to survive a conversion from your layout into someone else's data model intact.
Work through these in order. The first four account for most parsing failures we see.

items: Submit a PDF unless the posting says otherwise. Modern systems read PDFs reliably; the exception is a job board that explicitly asks for .docx.
Put contact details in the body, not the header. Some parsers skip document headers and footers entirely, which is how a resume arrives with no phone number attached.
Use one column. Two-column layouts are read left to right across the whole line, so your sidebar interleaves with your job history into nonsense.
Name sections conventionally. Experience, Education, Skills. A parser looks for these words; “Where I've Been” means nothing to it.
Write dates as MM/YYYY. Consistently, in every entry. Mixed formats produce gaps that look like unemployment.
Spell out an acronym once. “Search engine optimisation (SEO)” matches a recruiter searching for either.
Keep skills as text, not ratings. Five-star bars and progress rings carry no information the database can store.
Avoid tables for layout. Cell boundaries frequently vanish on parse, merging adjacent text.
Name the file properly. Firstname-Lastname-Role.pdf — it is the first thing a recruiter sees in a folder of two hundred.

blocks.text: Recruiters search the database with the language of the job description. If the posting says “stakeholder management” and your resume says “worked with lots of teams”, you are invisible to that search — not because you lack the skill, but because you named it differently.

The fix is narrow: mirror the posting's vocabulary where it genuinely matches what you did, inside real sentences about real outcomes. Do not paste a keyword block in white text at the bottom. Every recruiter has seen that trick, the parser reads it perfectly, and it ends the application.
I do not need your resume to be beautiful. I need to be able to find it six weeks from now when a role opens that fits you better.
blocks.attribution: A recruiter, on why structure beats design

blocks.title: The sixty-second check
items: Copy the text out of your own PDF and paste it into a plain notepad. If it reads in a sensible order, a parser will manage it.
Confirm your phone and email survived that paste.
Check every date format matches.
Read the job title in the posting and make sure it appears somewhere truthful on the page.

blocks.text: That paste test is the single most useful thing in this article. It shows you your resume the way the software sees it, in about a minute.

summary-that-earns-the-interview.title: Write a summary that earns the interview
summary-that-earns-the-interview.excerpt: The three lines at the top of your resume get more attention than anything else on the page — and are usually the least considered thing on it.

sections.title: Why those three lines carry so much

blocks.text: A first pass over a resume is fast — often well under a minute. In that pass the reader is answering one question: is this person plausibly right for the role? The summary is the only part of the page written specifically to answer it.

Which is why the generic version is so expensive. “Results-driven professional seeking a challenging opportunity” answers nothing. It could sit on top of any resume ever written, and the reader learns that you had nothing specific to say.
A summary that earns its space does three jobs in three sentences.

items: What you are, in the role's own words. “Backend engineer with six years in payments infrastructure.”
Your strongest proof. One concrete, quantified thing. “Rebuilt a settlement pipeline handling £40m a month, cutting reconciliation errors by 80%.”
Where you are pointed. One line connecting that history to this specific job — the only sentence you rewrite per application.

blocks.title: Rewrite one sentence, not the whole resume
blocks.text: Tailoring has a reputation for being slow because people rewrite everything. Change the third sentence and reorder your top two bullet points. That is ninety percent of the benefit for five percent of the effort.

sections.title: Words that are costing you space

blocks.text: Some phrases appear on nearly every resume, which means they distinguish you from nobody. Each one you cut buys room for something only you could write.

items: Results-driven, dynamic, passionate — claims with no evidence attached.
Team player — assert this with an outcome that required a team, or not at all.
Responsible for — describes the job description you were handed, not what you achieved in it.
Seeking a challenging position — everyone is. Say which position.

blocks.text: Replace every adjective about yourself with a number about your work. If you cannot find the number, the claim was probably not doing much.

choosing-the-right-template.title: How to choose a resume template you won't regret
choosing-the-right-template.excerpt: Template choice is mostly a question about your industry, not your taste. Here is how to read the room before you commit to a layout.

sections.title: A template is a signal, not a decoration

blocks.text: Before a word is read, the layout has already said something: how formal this field is, whether you understand its conventions, and how much of your case rests on visual craft. A design studio and a central bank are reading for opposite signals, and the same beautiful template fails one of them.
So the useful question is not “which template do I like?” but “what does a strong candidate in this field usually look like on paper?”

items: Finance, law, government, academia. Single column, restrained type, no colour blocks. Conservative is the correct answer, and length may run to two or three pages.
Engineering and data. Clean single column with a dense, scannable skills section. Substance over ornament; recruiters here scan for stack names first.
Design, brand, marketing. Layout is part of the portfolio. Take more visual licence — but keep the content parseable, because the ATS does not care that you are a designer.
Healthcare and education. Structured and credential-forward. Licences, registrations and dates need to be immediately findable.

blocks.title: When in doubt, go plainer
blocks.text: A restrained template is never the reason someone is rejected. An elaborate one occasionally is. Asymmetric risk should decide close calls.

One page is a norm for early careers, not a law. Ten years of relevant work compressed into one page in eight-point type is worse than two comfortable pages. The real constraint is that every line must earn its place.
Margins below about 1.5cm and body text below 10pt are the two reliable signs that a resume needs cutting rather than shrinking. If it does not fit, the fix is editing, not typography.

blocks.title: Quick sanity check
items: Squint at the page. Do the job titles stand out on their own?
Print it in greyscale. Does anything important disappear?
Hand it to someone outside your field for ten seconds, then ask what you do.

questions-hiding-in-your-resume.title: The interview questions hiding in your resume
questions-hiding-in-your-resume.excerpt: Most first-round questions are generated directly from the page you handed over. You can predict nearly all of them, and shape a few.

blocks.text: The honest version: many interviewers read your resume a few minutes before the call, marking the things that stand out. Gaps. Short tenures. Numbers that seem large. Anything vague enough to be worth probing. Those marks become the questions.
This is good news. The agenda is a document you wrote, so you can read it the way they will and prepare the specific conversation it invites.

sections.title: The four things that always get asked about

items: Any gap over three months. Answer it in one calm sentence and move on. Defensiveness is the only thing that makes a gap interesting.
Any number you quoted. If you wrote “increased conversion 34%”, expect “from what baseline, over what period, and what did you personally change?” Know all three.
Anything under a year. Give a forward-looking reason, not a grievance about the last employer.
The most impressive line on the page. It will be probed hardest. Make sure it is the achievement you can talk about longest.

blocks.title: The trap in your own bullet points
blocks.text: Never write a claim you cannot narrate for two minutes. A number you cannot explain reads as borrowed credit, and it costs more than the impressive figure ever gained.

Because the resume sets the agenda, you can deliberately leave one slightly under-explained line — a project with an unusual constraint, a result that sounds improbable. Curiosity does the rest, and you get asked about the thing you most wanted to discuss.
The candidate who has rehearsed the story behind every number is not over-prepared. They are prepared for the interview they scheduled.

ai-that-does-not-sound-like-ai.title: Building AI writing that doesn't sound like AI
ai-that-does-not-sound-like-ai.excerpt: A note from our product team on why generated resume copy so often reads like nothing at all, and the constraints we use to stop it.

blocks.text: Ask a general model to “improve” a resume bullet and you usually get something longer, smoother and emptier. “Managed the deployment pipeline” becomes “Spearheaded transformative initiatives to optimise deployment infrastructure, driving significant operational efficiencies.” Every specific has been traded for a superlative.
Recruiters spot this instantly, and it reads worse than the plain original — because the plain original at least described something that happened.

items: Never invent a number. If the model cannot find a metric in what you wrote, it asks you for one rather than producing a plausible-looking figure.
Rewrites may not get longer. A hard ceiling on output length removes the main route to padding.
Verbs come from a vetted list. No spearheading, no leveraging, no synergies.
Your voice is the baseline. Suggestions are edits to your sentence, not replacements written from scratch.

blocks.title: Why we ask before we write
blocks.text: The interesting detail is almost always in your head rather than your draft — the size of the team, the deadline, what broke. A question that surfaces it beats any amount of rewriting around its absence.

sections.title: How to get the most out of it

blocks.text: Write the ugly, factual version first. Bad grammar is fine. Include the numbers, the tools and the mess. Then ask for help tightening it. Editing beats generating, every time — and the result still sounds like a person, because a person wrote it.

blocks.title: In short
items: Draft badly but specifically.
Let the tool cut, not inflate.
Read every suggestion aloud before accepting it.
If you would not say it in an interview, do not put it on the page.

changing-career-without-starting-over.title: Changing career without starting over
changing-career-without-starting-over.excerpt: A career change resume is not a blank page. It is an argument, and the evidence is already in your history — filed under the wrong headings.

sections.title: You are making an argument, not listing a history

blocks.text: A chronological resume assumes the reader wants to know what you did in order. A career-change resume has a harder job: it must explain why a history in one field is evidence of capability in another. That is an argument, and arguments need structure.
The most common mistake is hiding the change. Vagueness does not conceal a career switch; it just removes the reasoning and leaves the reader to guess.

Go through your last two roles and separate what you did from the field you did it in. A teacher managing thirty pupils, a curriculum and a set of anxious parents has run stakeholder management, scheduling and performance reporting. The work transfers; only the vocabulary does not.

items: Lead with a summary that names the change. One sentence, stated plainly, giving the reason.
Add a short skills section immediately after it using the target field's language.
Reorder your bullet points so the transferable ones come first inside each role.
Show one piece of proof from the new field — a course, a freelance project, a volunteer build. Small and real beats large and hypothetical.

blocks.title: On functional resumes
blocks.text: Skills-first formats that drop dates look like concealment, and recruiters treat them that way. Keep the reverse-chronological spine and do the translating inside it.

You will be less experienced in the new field than someone who has been in it for a decade. Pretending otherwise is transparent. What you have instead is a decade of adjacent judgement and a genuinely different perspective — say that, once, plainly, and let the proof carry the rest.
Nobody hires a career changer by accident. If they are reading your resume, they are already open to the idea — your only job is to make it easy to say yes.
